commit.message:
channeldb: scope confirmation hints by script

In this commit, we key confirmation hints by the same txid and output
script that a confirmation request uses to match a transaction. Two
pending requests can share a txid while watching different scripts,
and the txid-only cache key let one request's scan advance the other's
hint, so the request could resume from its caller-provided height
instead of the block where its transaction confirmed.

We add a cache regression for requests with the same txid and different
scripts, plus an integration case that runs the breach confirmation
with bitcoind without txindex and requires the justice transaction to
sweep the revoked outputs while the funding request remains pending.

commit.message:
docs: explain the remote signer modes by who dials

The introduction described the two modes in terms of inbound and
outbound connections without saying that the labels are from the
signer's point of view, leaving a reader to discover the inversion when
they meet remotesigner.experimentalallowinboundconnection and wonder why
an "outbound" remote signer needs an "allow inbound" option.

Lead with the only thing that actually differs between the modes, which
is which node dials, give it as a table, then explain whose perspective
the labels take and warn that they invert on the other side.

commit.message:
lnd: clarify which connection the dedicated signer server accepts

The dedicated RPC server exists to accept the connection a remote signer
dials to this watch-only node. The comments called it "the inbound
watch-only signer stream" and similar, which requires the reader to
already know that "inbound" is from this node's point of view and not
the signer's.

Say what the server does instead, and make the startup error name the
server by its purpose rather than by the ambiguous adjective.

commit.message:
lncfg: describe the remote signer modes by who dials

Say which node dials the other in the comments on
ExperimentalAllowInboundConnection, InboundWatchOnlyCfg, ConnectionCfg
and the credential validation, rather than leaving the reader to work
out whose perspective "inbound" is from.

The experimentalrpclisten description is the one worth calling out. It
read "Dedicated RPC listen address(es) for inbound remote signer
connections", which parses just as naturally as "connections to an
inbound remote signer" - the opposite mode, and one where this option
does nothing. It now says the listeners are where this node accepts the
connection dialled by a remote signer.

Also fixes the grammar in the WatchOnlyNode.ExperimentalEnable comment.

commit.message:
rpcwallet: say which node dials instead of inbound/outbound

"Inbound" and "outbound" name the same connection differently depending
on which side you read them from, and the comments in this package
alternated between the two perspectives without saying which one they
meant. The result was documentation that is technically correct and very
easy to misread, which the review of #8754 called out specifically.

The clearest example was the connection builder, whose doc comment said
that an inbound remote signer yields an OutboundConnection and an
outbound remote signer yields an InboundConnection. Both statements are
true, and neither helps a reader who does not already know the
convention.

Rewrite the comments to state who dials whom, and where the words are
kept, say whose point of view they are from. The type names are
deliberately left alone; renaming them is a larger change and the review
suggested only considering it later if the terminology keeps causing
confusion.

Also fixes the Build comment on RemoteSignerClientBuilder, which
referred to an OutboundRemoteSignerClient type that does not exist, and
a typo in the InboundRemoteSignerConnection comment.

commit.message:
rpcwallet: call the startup timeout by its name

SignCoordinator and InboundConnection held the value configured as
remotesigner.experimentalstartuptimeout in a field named
connectionTimeout. That name belongs to a different timeout: lncfg's
ConnectionCfg.Timeout, which bounds a single attempt at establishing an
outbound connection. Reading the coordinator in isolation, the field
looked like the latter.

Rename the field and the constructor parameters to startupTimeout, and
say in the comments that 0 means wait indefinitely, which the zero check
in WaitUntilConnected implements but did not state.

InboundConnection.Timeout keeps its name, as it satisfies the
RemoteSignerConnection interface, but its comment now says which timeout
it returns and why that is the only connection-related one that applies
when the signer dials us.

No functional change.

commit.message:
lncfg: clarify the three remote signer timeout descriptions

A remote signing setup has three separately configured timeouts, and the
config help did not make clear which phase each one bounds. The startup
timeout's description also contained the sentence "If set to 0, no
timeout will not expire", which says the opposite of what it means.

Describe each timeout by the phase it bounds and cross-reference the
others, so an operator reading any one of them can tell it apart from
the rest:

  - the startup timeout waits for the signer to connect to us, applies
    only in inbound mode, and 0 means wait indefinitely
  - the connection timeout bounds a single attempt at opening the
    connection, and has no effect on a watch-only node accepting an
    inbound connection
  - the request timeout bounds a single request over a connection that
    is already up

Give the three default constants comments in the same terms.

commit.message:
docs: document the remote signing security model

The remote signing doc explained how to split a node into a watch-only
instance and a signer, but not what that split actually guarantees. The
natural reading of "watch-only" is that compromising such a node is
harmless, and that is not the case.

The signer forwards every request straight to its local signrpc and
walletrpc sub-servers. It does not inspect what it is asked to sign, and
there is no allow-list of destinations, amounts or key paths. An attacker
who controls the watch-only node can therefore obtain a valid signature
over a transaction that sweeps the wallet, without ever touching a
private key.

Add a Security model section covering what the split does protect
against, what it does not, the assumptions it makes about the watch-only
node, and the operational isolation that follows from them.

Link to the new section from the introduction, where a reader first
forms an impression of what the setup buys them.

commit.message:
lnwallet: fix lint issues in force close changes

In this commit, we rewrap the overlong comment, test name, and restart
call in the channel arbitrator restart test, keep a blank line before
the early return, split the long force close errorf in brontide, and
move the restored-status check in the force close guard into its own
expression so the multi-line condition formats cleanly.
docs: add release note for restored channels

lnwallet: reject force close for restored channels

In this commit, we prevent restored channel shells from entering the local force-close path. These shells do not have a local commitment transaction, so attempting to sign one can panic and leave the arbitrator in a persisted broadcast state.

We treat the restored status like local data loss and let the arbitrator wait for the remote close. We also handle the resulting nil close transaction in the peer failure path instead of dereferencing it for logging.
